1:
Calvin thinks the chapter begins in the wrong place: the division interrupts one of the most touching scenes in the sacred volume just in the middle, separating the irresistible appeal of Judah from its happy effect, whereas in the Hebrew Bible the section commences with Judah's address and the whole is one continuous narrative. Joseph had done violence to his feelings so long as he presented an austere countenance; at length the affection he had suppressed while breathing threatenings poured itself forth with the more abundant force, whence it appears that nothing cruel had before been harboured in his mind; and that it bursts forth in tears deserves more praise than an equable temper would. The stoics therefore speak foolishly in saying it an heroic virtue not to be touched with compassion — had Joseph stood inflexible, who would not have pronounced him iron-hearted? By the vehemence of his feelings he manifests rather a noble magnanimity, being so superior to anger that he ardently loved those who had conspired to effect his ruin. He commanded all men to depart not because he was ashamed of his kindred, since he afterwards permits the report to be carried to the palace, but because he would not make known their crime before many witnesses; it was not the smallest part of his clemency to desire their disgrace wholly buried in oblivion.

Henry, whom Wesley follows almost word for word, reads the scene as a picture of grace. Judah and his brethren, waiting for an answer, could not but be amazed to discover, instead of the gravity of a judge, the natural affection of a brother. The private conversations of friends are the most free: when Joseph would put on love he puts off state, and it was not fit his servants should be witnesses of it — thus Christ manifests his loving-kindness to his people out of the sight and hearing of the world. The tears were the introduction to his discourse. He had dammed up this stream a great while, but now it swelled so high that he wept aloud, so that those whom he had forbidden to see him could not but hear him; and with these tears he threw off the austerity with which he had hitherto carried himself. Then abruptly, as one uneasy till it was out, he tells them who he is. They knew him only by his Egyptian name, his Hebrew name being lost in Egypt, and lest they suspect another of the same name he explains himself — I am Joseph your brother — which would both humble them for their sin and encourage them to hope for kind treatment.

Clarke fastens on the verb, which is very emphatic: it signifies to force one's self, to do something against nature. Joseph could no longer constrain himself to act a feigned part — all the brother and the son rose up in him at once and overpowered his resolutions; he felt for his father, realising his agony, and for his brethren, now at his feet submissive in distress; and that he might give free scope to his affectionate heart he ordered the attendants out. Clarke quotes Dodd, that the beauties of this chapter are so striking it would be an indignity to point them out, nothing in sacred or profane history being more highly wrought up. Ellicott names what overpowered him: the picture Judah had drawn of his father's love for Benjamin, the thought that by separating them he might have made his father die of grief, and the sight of Judah offering to endure slavery for him. He cleared the room so that there might be no restraint on either side when he told them he was the brother they had condemned to slavery. Gill notes only that Judah's speech had such an effect on his passions that he could no longer refrain from tears.
2:
That the weeping carried so far puzzles Clarke, since Joseph's dwelling was presumably not near the palace, and he answers it out of travel. Sir John Chardin, he reports, says this is exactly the genius of the people of Asia: their sentiments of joy or grief are properly transports, ungoverned and excessive. When anyone returns from a long journey, or dies, his family burst into cries that may be heard twenty doors off, renewed at intervals and continuing many days. Clarke allows two soberer readings — that the house of Pharaoh may mean the king's servants, such as those just dismissed, still within hearing, or that the report was afterwards brought to the palace. Ellicott takes the last flatly: what the Egyptians and the house of Pharaoh heard was not the weeping but the news that his brethren had come. Keil reads it the other way, that as soon as the rest were gone Joseph broke out into such loud weeping that the Egyptians outside could hear it. Gill observes that the restraint he had put on himself made the flood the greater and his voice the louder.

The brothers' silence Calvin turns into a rule for dealing with the penitent. Although Joseph had given the clearest token of his mildness, yet when he told them his name they were terrified as if he had thundered against them; for while they revolve what they have deserved, his power seems so formidable that they anticipate nothing but death. Seeing them overcome with fear, he utters no reproach, but labours to calm their perturbation, and soothes them until he has rendered them composed and cheerful. By this example we are taught lest sadness overwhelm those truly humbled under a sense of shame. So long as the offender is deaf to reproofs, or flatters himself, or excuses himself by hypocrisy, greater severity is to be used; but rigour should have its bounds, and as soon as he trembles under the sense of his sin, that moderation should follow which may raise him by the hope of pardon. Keil notices that Joseph asks after his father although twice told he was living, his filial heart impelling him to make sure once more, and that the brothers were so smitten in conscience they could not utter a word. Gill supposes the name itself startling, since they had known him, if at all, only as Zaphnath-paaneah.

The invitation to come near is, in Calvin's judgment, more efficacious than words. Joseph attempers his speech so that he mildly accuses and again consoles them, but the consolation predominates, because he sees them on the point of desperation; and in mentioning the selling he does not renew their guilt to expostulate, but because it is profitable that the sense of sin remain, provided terror does not absorb a man after he has acknowledged his fault. Since they were more than sufficiently terrified, he insists the more on healing the wound, repeating that God had sent him for their preservation, and that he had not been sent into Egypt by them but led thither by the hand of God — and this when only two years of the famine had passed and five remained in which there should be neither ploughing nor harvest. Ellicott finds much force in the assurance that he was still their brother, for they stood speechless at finding the hated dreamer, on whose anguish they had looked unmoved, now ruler of a mighty empire. Gill supposes they had kept their distance while he sat in state, so that the summons brought them near enough to speak privately and to discern in his face the features they had known. Clarke sets the scene beside Homer, where Ulysses discovers himself to Telemachus — I am thy father, for whose sake thou lead'st a life of woe — and tears till then restrained trickle down the cheeks of both.
5:
Calvin calls this a remarkable passage, teaching that the course of events is never so disturbed by the wickedness of men but that God can direct it to a good end — and teaching also how we must consider providence. When men of inquisitive minds dispute about it they invent every absurdity to sully the justice of God, and that rashness makes some pious men wish the doctrine concealed; yet a just measure must be kept, lest we encourage ignorance of what the word of God makes plain. Good men, afraid of exposing God's justice to the calumnies of the impious, resort to the distinction that God permits some things but does others — as if any liberty of action were left to men were he to cease governing. Away with that vain figment, Calvin says, that by permission only and not by will those evils are committed which God afterwards turns to good account. The vice dwells in the men, and the blame is theirs; but God works wonderfully through their means, that from their impurity he may bring forth his righteousness. The example is before our eyes: Joseph was sold by his brethren for no reason but that they wished to ruin him, and the same work is ascribed to God for a very different end — God willing that Joseph should be as one dead for a short time, that he might suddenly bring him forth from the grave as the preserver of life. Though at the outset he seems to do the same thing as the wicked, there is a wide distance between their wickedness and his admirable judgment.

The title Joseph gives himself interests the commentators. Clarke conjectures that father was a name of office in Egypt, signifying what prime minister does among us; Calmet remarks that among the Phoenicians, Persians, Arabians and Romans the title was given to officers of state, and Clarke adds from Diodorus that the counsellors of the kings of Egypt were chosen out of the priesthood. Ellicott agrees that this was a common title of the vizier of Oriental kings, and notices a smaller thing: the article is rarely found with Elohim in the history of Joseph, but wherever it is added it marks deep feeling in the speaker — it was the God whom their race had worshipped that had now interposed to save them. Keil renders the office Pharaoh's most confidential counsellor. Gill guards the denial that they sent him: not absolutely, since they did sell him to the Ishmaelites, but comparatively, providence having overruled those events.

Wesley draws the lesson. God's Israel is the particular care of God's providence, and Joseph reckoned his advancement designed not so much to save a whole kingdom of Egyptians as to preserve a small family of Israelites; for the Lord's portion is his people, and whatever goes with others they shall be secured. How admirable are the projects of providence, how remote its tendencies. Clarke reads the words with every emphasis: not you but God, not you that sold me but God who sent me; Egypt and Canaan must both have perished had not a merciful provision been made. Ellicott weighs the promise itself. To preserve a posterity is, in Hebrew, to put for them a remnant in the land, for during the famine many races probably dwindled away, and the Hebrews, as sojourners in Canaan, would have been in danger of extinction; and where the first clause seems to forebode that few would survive, the word rendered deliverance, which signifies rather that which escapes, assures them of surviving in numbers enough to grow into a great nation. On the word earing both note the old English for ploughing, and Clarke adds that the promise of no seed-time must be qualified, since the Egyptians afterwards came to buy seed, and ground on the river's borders was probably still sown.
9:
Calvin explains why Joseph presses his own greatness. In giving this command he speaks of his power in order to inspire his father with stronger confidence: we know how dilatory old men are, and besides it was difficult to tear holy Jacob away from the inheritance divinely promised him. It may be asked why the old oracle did not occur to their minds, that they should be strangers and servants in a strange land, since Joseph seems to promise nothing but pleasures. Moses says nothing, but Calvin conjectures that Jacob was not forgetful of it; for unless he had been retained by some celestial chain he could never have remained in Egypt after the scarcity was over, since by remaining voluntarily he would have appeared to cast away the hope of the inheritance. Seeing that he does not provide for his return but only commands his corpse to be carried thither, nor exhorts his sons to return but suffers them to settle, he does this not from indolence, but because he is preparing himself and his offspring to bear that tyranny of which Isaac had forewarned him. He regards it as an advantage that at his first coming he is hospitably received; but meanwhile he revolves in his mind what had been spoken to Abraham.

Goshen the commentators locate as best they can. Clarke supposes the district had been allotted to Joseph by the king, since otherwise he could scarcely have promised it without Pharaoh's consent; it was the most easterly province of Lower Egypt, lying next to Canaan, and is also called the land of Rameses from a city of that name. Because the Hebrew for rain is a similar word, Jerome and others supposed Goshen was so named because it had rain, unlike Egypt in general; being watered from heaven might account for its being the best of the land. Ellicott places it on the eastern bank of the Nile, commencing a little north of Memphis and extending to the Mediterranean; it was probably an unsettled district, rich in pastures, belonging in a very loose way to Egypt, and there the Israelites were constantly joined by Semitic immigrants enrolled among their dependants. Gill identifies it with the Heliopolitan nome, which Strabo reckoned to be in Arabia, and wonders whether Joseph had a grant of it or whether it was the domain of his father-in-law the priest of On.

The proofs Joseph offers are of the plainest kind. Gill says the brothers were eyewitnesses that he was alive, and Benjamin with them, who could not be suspected by his father of a fraud; and Wesley, that if they could recollect themselves they might remember something of his features and speech. Clarke thinks he laid considerable stress on speaking with them in Hebrew without an interpreter, as the Targum of Jonathan renders it, that it was his own mouth that spoke with them in the language of the house of the sanctuary. Ellicott reckons the household that would come down with Jacob: as the famine had lasted only two years and he had preserved his flocks, he had probably lost few of his servants, and would go down as head of a large tribe called Israelites after him — a name of subjection as much as of descent. On the embrace, Clarke notes that among the Asiatics kissing the beard, neck and shoulders is in use to this day, so that falling on the neck signifies no more than kissing it with the arms around; and Gill, that the word for neck is plural, so that Joseph may have fallen first on one side and then the other. Keil marks the sequence: only after Joseph had by a triple assurance dispelled their fear of retribution, and sealed his words by embracing and kissing them with tears, did his brethren talk with him.
16:
Henry dwells on Pharaoh's kindness to Joseph and, for his sake, to his relations. He bade the brethren welcome though it was a time of scarcity and they were likely to be a charge to him; and because it pleased Pharaoh it pleased his servants too, or at least they pretended so. He engaged Joseph to send for his father and promised every convenience for the removal and the settlement: if the good of all the land of Egypt would suffice them they were welcome to it all, even the fat of the land. Pharaoh was respectful to Joseph in gratitude, Henry adds, because he had been an instrument of much good to his kingdom, since the neighbours would say that surely the Egyptians are a wise people to be so well stocked in a time of scarcity; and there is a gratitude owing even to inferiors, to be requited not only to our benefactors but to their relations. What they had in Canaan he reckoned but stuff beside what awaited them, and if they left some behind they need not be discontented, for Egypt would make up the losses of the removal. Thus, Henry says, those for whom Christ intends shares in his heavenly glory ought not to regard the stuff of this world: its best enjoyments are but stuff, but lumber, which we cannot make sure of here, much less carry away; better things are reserved in that blessed land whither our Joseph has gone to prepare a place.

Calvin points out that the order of the narrative is not the order of events. Before Joseph sent for his father the report of his brethren's coming had reached the palace, and he would not have promised them a home so confidently except by the king's permission; the king had with a ready mind declared his esteem for Joseph by freely offering his father and brethren the most fertile part of Egypt. From another statement of Moses it appears that as long as this king lived the Israelites were treated with clemency, the beginning of the tyranny being ascribed to his successor, to whom Joseph was unknown. Ellicott sees the point of recording the welcome so fully: it mattered greatly for their future position that the Israelites should go into Egypt not as men who had forced themselves on the country but as invited guests. Gill supposes the report reached court from some of Joseph's household who had overheard what passed, and that Joseph afterwards waited on Pharaoh himself, the king being unlikely to give such orders on a rumour.

The provision for the journey turns on two details. Keil notes that Egypt was from time immemorial rich in small two-wheeled carriages usable even where there were no roads, and that Pharaoh empowered Joseph to give his brethren such carriages for the children, the wives and their aged father. Ellicott says the same from the monuments: Egypt being flat and carefully cultivated was adapted for vehicles, those depicted having two wheels and being drawn by oxen, while the chariots of Pharaoh and Joseph were probably drawn by horses, then newly introduced. He distinguishes the little ones from the household — the Hebrew covers the whole mass of dependants, and where the household means chiefly the men, this term would be the female slaves and the children. On the stuff, Clarke renders it literally, let not your eye spare your vessels, a general term taking in household furniture and agricultural utensils: they were not to encumber themselves with articles readily found in Egypt. Ellicott and Keil render the idiom the same way, that the eye should not look with pity on the goods. Gill records a contrary construction, that the words mean rather to leave nothing behind but bring all away, as though Joseph would not have them think of returning; he judges it agrees less well with what follows.
21:
Calvin asks why Joseph loaded his brethren with money and garments when they would soon return, and answers that he did it on account of his father and their wives, that they might be the less reluctant to leave Canaan; for he knew his message would scarcely be believed unless manifest tokens of its truth were presented. On the changes of raiment he differs from the tradition: Jerome translated the phrase two robes, and others follow him, but Calvin supposes rather elegant garments such as were used at weddings and on festal days. Clarke sets the gift among Eastern usages, since the Asiatic sovereigns keep hundreds of changes of raiment ready as presents for those they honour; Ellicott says the brethren would show by their very apparel how honourable their treatment had been.

The caution against falling out engages every voice. Wesley, following Henry, knows they were too apt to be quarrelsome, and what had lately passed might give them occasion; so Joseph, having forgiven them all, lays them under an obligation not to upbraid each other. This charge our Lord has given us too, that whatever former occurrences are remembered we fall not out — for we are brethren and have all one Father; we are guilty, verily guilty, and have more reason to fall out with ourselves; and we are by the way, a way that lies through Egypt, where many eyes seek advantage against us, and leads to Canaan, where we hope to be for ever in perfect peace. Calvin notes that the Hebrew word may mean either to tremble or to make a tumult, and thinks the latter the more appropriate: Joseph was pacified towards them, but admonishes them not to stir up strife, since each, in excusing himself, would be likely to lay the blame on others. Christ requires his disciples to be not only lovers of peace but peace-makers. Ellicott reports that several moderns render the clause be not afraid of the journey, but on insufficient grounds.

The homecoming Henry treats in two stages, and Wesley after him. The relation of it at first sank Jacob's spirits: when without any preamble his sons came in crying that Joseph was yet alive, perhaps he thought they bantered him, or the mention of the name revived his sorrow, so that his heart fainted. That Joseph is alive is too good news to be true, and he faints because he believes it not — for we faint because we do not believe. Calvin agrees that this was no simple affection of joy but a mingled perturbation: Moses does not say he was suffocated by sudden gladness, as some suppose, but that having no confidence in his sons he was held in suspense between hope and fear. Ellicott reads the fainting as surprise rather than incredulity: Jacob, crushed by the loss of the child who had taken Rachel's place, could not open his mind to the tidings, whose first effect was to chill him with a renewed sense of loss. What restored him was the sight of the wagons, seeing being believing; and Clarke notes that the Greek word for his reviving signifies the blowing up of almost extinguished embers, the word Paul uses for stirring up the gift of God. Gill supposes what the brothers reported was not their selling of him, which Jacob perhaps never heard, but Joseph's advancement; Keil, that his heart did not beat at the news, for he put no faith in it. With the wagons before him, Henry says, Jacob is called Israel again, for he begins to recover his wonted vigour: it pleases him to think that Joseph is alive, and he says nothing of the glory they had told him of, for it was enough to him that Joseph was alive — and those who would be content with less degrees of comfort are best prepared for greater.
28:
What moved the old man, Clarke insists, was not the dignity but the life. It was not the state to which Joseph had risen; it was that he was still alive, and this that made him exclaim, much! multiplied! my son is yet alive! I will go and see him before I die. Gill takes the exclamation the same way: the word is much or great, and the Targums render it that he had much joy — it was more to him than all Joseph's splendour that he was in the land of the living. Though his age was great and the journey long, so strong was his desire of seeing Joseph that he determined at once upon going, expecting death shortly; and Gill supposes the resolution made in submission to God's will, since he wished to live only to enjoy this favour. Ellicott would not lay too much stress on the change of name, as though Israel were a title fit only for the patriarch's happier hours, since it is given him earlier in the chapter in the midst of his distress; both names were long in use of him personally. But because Israel alone was the name given to Jacob's family, a high significance was plainly attached to it, and the inheritance of the Abrahamic promises was early connected with it.

Clarke closes the chapter with four reflections on Joseph's conduct, several things in it being hard to account for. It is strange, knowing how much his father loved him, that he never took one of the many opportunities to let him know he was alive, since his father would undoubtedly have paid his ransom. But prudence dictated secrecy: his brethren, jealous in the extreme, would soon have found other methods of destroying his life had they got him again into their power, so that for his safety he chose rather to be a bond-slave in Egypt than to risk returning home. His carriage to his brethren before making himself known appears inexcusably harsh, if not vindictive; but when the men are considered it is evident that no other means would have awakened their torpid consciences — a desperate disease requires a desperate remedy, and the event justified all that he did.

The hardest of the four, Clarke owns, is the demand that Benjamin be torn away from the bleeding heart of an aged and desolate father in whose affection Joseph had himself long lived. Unless the Spirit of prophecy had assured him the experiment would end favourably, his conduct in making it cannot well be vindicated; learned men have attributed it to such a prophetic intimation, and this consideration, if it does not untie the knot, at least cuts it. Perhaps it is best to say that Joseph acted as directed by a providence under whose influence he might have been led to do many things he had not designed, the issue proving that God's wisdom governed every circumstance. Of the chapter itself Clarke speaks warmly. The speech of Joseph to his brethren is inferior only to that of Judah in the chapter before, and the whole heart of the affectionate brother is seen in the delicacy of the apology he makes for them, art being swallowed up by nature — be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves; it was not you that sent me hither, but God. The whole chapter, he says, is a masterpiece, the more impressive because it is evidently a simple relation of facts just as they occurred, with no attempt to heighten the effect by rhetorical colouring: it is sheer nature throughout, a history that has no fellow, where every one acts up to his own character and nothing is extravagant in degree. Gill ends on another note, that in making himself known Joseph was a type of Christ, who manifests himself to his people and not to the world.
